lessons.title: Neonatal Transition & Initial Steps: first minute matters
lessons.summary: Neonatal resuscitation differs from PALS: most bradycardia at birth is due to ineffective ventilation/gas exchange. Effective lung inflation is the central intervention.

sections.title: 1) Transition physiology
paragraphs: At birth pulmonary vascular resistance falls, lungs aerate and oxygen saturation rises gradually over minutes. Newborn targets are therefore lower than older children/adults in the first minutes.

sections.title: 2) Initial questions
paragraphs: Term gestation? good tone? breathing/crying? If yes → routine care/temperature/ongoing evaluation. If no → warm, dry, position, stimulate, clear airway only if needed.

sections.title: 3) When to ventilate
paragraphs: Apnea/gasping or HR <100/min → begin positive-pressure ventilation promptly. Rise in heart rate is the best indicator of effective ventilation.

sections.title: 4) Oxygen strategy
paragraphs: 2025 AHA/AAP: term/late preterm ≥35 wk can reasonably start respiratory support with 21% O₂; 32–34+6 wk 21–30%; <32 wk may need 30–100%, titrated to preductal SpO₂ targets.

key_points: HR response tells you if ventilation works

research_updates.title: 2025 Neonatal Resuscitation emphasizes cord/transition systems
research_updates.takeaway: The 2025 AHA/AAP neonatal guideline introduces an updated algorithm and Newborn Chain of Care, with emphasis on cord-management planning, thermal care and effective ventilation.

quiz.q: Key indicator of effective PPV in newborn?
quiz.explain: A rising heart rate is the primary indicator of effective ventilation.

lessons.title: Neonatal Ventilation, ETT, Laryngeal Mask & Video Laryngoscopy
lessons.summary: Airway newborn ต้องคิดตาม GA/weight, device availability และ ventilation effectiveness. New 2025 evidence strengthens the role of supraglottic airway and video laryngoscopy in selected settings.

sections.title: 1) Face-mask ventilation problems
paragraphs: Mask leak and airway obstruction are common. If HR stays <100/min despite PPV, perform corrective ventilation steps and consider alternative airway.

sections.title: 2) Laryngeal mask
paragraphs: 2025 guidance: laryngeal mask is reasonable as an alternative to ETT when face-mask ventilation fails in newborns ≥34 weeks, and may be reasonable as a primary ventilation interface in that group where training/resources support it.

sections.title: 3) ETT sizing & depth
paragraphs: Use GA/weight table rather than one universal formula. Prepare adjacent tube sizes and confirm depth by clinical response/exhaled CO₂ and local imaging where appropriate.

sections.title: 4) Video laryngoscopy evidence
paragraphs: ILCOR 2025 suggests video laryngoscopy over traditional laryngoscopy where resources/training allow, especially for less-experienced clinicians. Meta-analysis of RCTs showed higher overall and first-attempt success.

sections.title: 5) Blade selection
paragraphs: Straight Miller-type blades are standard neonatal tools; #00 for extremely preterm/small infants in some systems, #0 for preterm, #1 for term/larger infants, but exact device choice should follow local equipment and training.

key_points: Video laryngoscopy improves first-attempt success in neonatal evidence
quick_review: Preterm often Miller 0; term often Miller 1

research_updates.title: Neonatal video laryngoscopy evidence
research_updates.takeaway: Across 4 RCTs, video laryngoscopy increased overall and first-attempt intubation success; ILCOR 2025 conditionally favors VL where resources/training permit.

research_updates.title: NICU quality improvement with VL
research_updates.takeaway: A 2026 QI project reported sustained improvement in first-attempt success after implementing VL and standardized oxygenation, including infants <1000 g.

quiz.q: 2025 neonatal guidance supports laryngeal mask most clearly in which group?
quiz.explain: Evidence and recommendations are strongest for newborns ≥34 weeks.
RCT evidence summarized by ILCOR showed improved first-attempt success.

lessons.title: Advanced Neonatal Resuscitation: compressions, epinephrine, volume, post-care
lessons.summary: เมื่อ HR ยัง <60/min หลัง ventilation ที่ทำให้ chest movement แล้ว ให้ escalate อย่างเป็นลำดับ: alternative airway → compressions 3:1 → oxygen/vascular access → epinephrine → causes/volume.

sections.title: 1) Chest compressions
paragraphs: If HR remains <60/min despite 30 s effective ventilation, provide chest compressions. Preferred technique = two-thumb encircling hands, ratio 3:1 with ventilation.

sections.title: 2) Epinephrine
paragraphs: If HR remains <60/min despite 60 s compressions + adequate ventilation, give intravascular epinephrine 0.01–0.03 mg/kg. ET epinephrine 0.05–0.1 mg/kg may be used while obtaining vascular access. Repeat q3–5 min if needed.

sections.title: 3) Vascular access
paragraphs: Low-lying umbilical venous catheter is preferred; IO may be considered when IV/UVC not feasible, depending on setting and expertise.

sections.title: 4) Volume expansion
paragraphs: When blood loss/hypovolemia is suspected and there is inadequate response to epinephrine, volume expansion is indicated; choice/volume follow neonatal/local protocol.

sections.title: 5) Postresuscitation
paragraphs: Monitor glucose, temperature, oxygenation/ventilation, neurologic status and complications after prolonged ventilation/advanced resuscitation.

quiz.explain: Effective ventilation must be established first; compressions are for persistent HR <60/min.

lessons.title: Neonatal Thermal Care & Oxygen Targets
lessons.summary: newborn resuscitation begins with transition physiology, temperature control and appropriate oxygen—not automatic 100% oxygen.

sections.title: 1) Transition
paragraphs: At birth, lung fluid clearance, aeration and fall in pulmonary vascular resistance allow pulmonary blood flow to rise. Effective ventilation is the key intervention when transition fails.

sections.title: 2) Temperature
paragraphs: Hypothermia increases oxygen consumption and worsens outcomes. Use warm environment, drying/skin-to-skin for stable term infants and additional thermal measures for preterm infants.

sections.title: 3) Oxygen
paragraphs: Use preductal pulse oximetry when resuscitation requires oxygen/ventilation and titrate according to neonatal target ranges and gestational context.

sections.title: 4) Cord management
paragraphs: 2025 guidance emphasizes a cord-management plan; deferred cord clamping is appropriate in many newborns who do not require immediate resuscitative intervention.

lessons.title: Neonatal Positive-Pressure Ventilation: The Most Important Skill
lessons.summary: Most neonatal bradycardia is caused by inadequate gas exchange; effective ventilation is the central resuscitation intervention.

sections.title: 1) When to ventilate
paragraphs: Apnea/gasping or HR <100/min after initial steps generally triggers ventilation in the neonatal algorithm.

sections.title: 2) Effectiveness
paragraphs: Look for rising HR and chest movement. If HR does not improve, correct mask seal/position, airway obstruction and ventilation technique before assuming medication is needed.

sections.title: 3) Corrective steps
paragraphs: Reposition airway, improve seal, suction if obstructed, adjust pressure and consider alternative airway when mask ventilation is ineffective.

sections.title: 4) Escalation
paragraphs: If HR remains <60/min despite effective ventilation, advanced airway and coordinated compressions are considered; ensure ventilation truly is effective first.

lessons.title: Post-Resuscitation Care of the Newborn
lessons.summary: ROSC/HR recovery does not end risk: monitor glucose, temperature, oxygenation and neurologic status.

sections.title: 1) Ongoing transition
paragraphs: Infants who required significant resuscitation can deteriorate again from respiratory disease, hypoglycemia, hypothermia, pulmonary hypertension or neurologic injury.

sections.title: 2) Monitoring
paragraphs: Temperature, glucose, oxygenation/ventilation, perfusion and neurologic state need continued observation.

sections.title: 3) Communication
paragraphs: Document timing/interventions, communicate with neonatal team and family, and perform team debriefing.

sections.title: 4) Higher-level care
paragraphs: Prolonged ventilation/compressions/epinephrine or persistent abnormal physiology warrants neonatal intensive care evaluation.
